Using data collected by the LHCb experiment at the LHC, we have assessed the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay rate, which is related to the effective lifespan of $B^0_s$ mesons. Our analysis of 3.0 inverse picobarns of data from 2011 and 5.0 inverse picobarns from 2012 yielded an assessment of the lifespan-related parameter, $\Gamma_{B^0_s} \Gamma_{K^+K^-}$, which is $1.14 \pm 0.08 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.04 \times 10^{-4}$ picoelectronvolts. This result is expressed as $1.14 \pm 0.12$ in units of $\Gamma_{B^0_s}$. Our findings are consistent with theoretical predictions and previous measurements.

This research focuses on a discrete model of a control system affected by a Lévy process, where the goal is to minimize the expected value of a cost function that combines the squared difference between a dynamic variable and a target value over time, plus the expected magnitude of a control measure. By leveraging the properties of semigroups, we establish that this system has a unique solution and establish its smoothness characteristics. Furthermore, we investigate the continuous nature of this solution with respect to specific parameters. To support these findings, numerical experiments are conducted using a discrete method.

The Pierre Auger Observatory has been monitoring the composition and direction of high-energy cosmic rays since 2004. Researchers analyzed data from 2004 to 2016 to understand the anisotropy of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays in different energy ranges. They found that anisotropy patterns change significantly at an energy threshold of 10 EeV, with a 12-degree dipole anisotropy observed in the highest energy range and no significant anisotropy in the lower energy range. The analysis also revealed a 10% increase in the likelihood of a common anisotropy pattern across the two energy ranges. The observed anisotropy is too large to be caused by the Milky Way and is likely influenced by nearby sources or large-scale magnetic fields.
This paper proves that all Zinbiel algebras possess a maximal solvable subalgebra, thereby demonstrating that they are inherently solvable.

A study was conducted to investigate the fluctuations in flow coefficients, specifically $v_2$ and $v_3$, in lead-lead collisions at the LHC with a total center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of 5.02 TeV. The analysis utilized 100,000 events from the ALICE experiment to examine the distribution of these fluctuations. The results showed that the width of the $v_2$ and $v_3$ distributions is primarily influenced by the initial geometry fluctuations, with the impact of event-by-event fluctuations in particle production being relatively minor. The study also investigated the relationship between $v_2$ and $v_3$, finding that the width of this correlation is mainly determined by the impact parameter fluctuations. The analysis further examined the impact of flow intensity fluctuations on the effective mass of pions and protons, finding that the width of the effective mass distributions is mainly influenced by the $v_2$ and $v_3$ fluctuations, with a minor contribution from thermal slope fluctuations.

This study focuses on resolving inconsistencies in tables that contain
empty cells and functional dependencies, which are discrepancies that occur
when the values in a cell do not match the defined relationship. We first
examine existing methods for managing such discrepancies, which are primarily
based on removing or altering the offending values. We then propose a novel
approach that views discrepancies as independent entities with their own
attributes, and employs a graph-based representation to capture the
relationships between them. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach
through a case study and provide a prototype implementation.

This research introduces a novel statistical model called the temporal varying Poisson autoregressive (TVPAR) model, designed to address dynamic relationships in discrete data. Building on the Poisson autoregressive framework, the model incorporates time-varying coefficients to capture evolving relationships and employs a flexible selection method for relevant lagged variables. The study develops the theoretical underpinnings of the TVPAR model, including its dynamic properties and estimation techniques. To illustrate the TVPAR model's effectiveness, the research presents both simulation experiments and an analysis of real-world data, specifically focusing on the temporal dynamics of crime rates in New York City.

To address the challenge of data-scarce 3D object modeling, we introduce Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel approach that represents objects using compact, rotation-invariant descriptors. NDFs consist of a set of point descriptors, each comprising a feature vector and covariance matrix, which collectively capture an object's geometry and uncertainty. This representation is particularly well-suited for integrating diverse data sources, such as CAD models and point clouds, and enables the creation of probabilistic descriptions of objects. We develop a method to generate such representations from point clouds and a corresponding network for volumetric object reconstruction. Our approach is validated on multiple datasets, including ShapeNet, T-SCAN, and ModelNet, demonstrating its ability to handle complex 3D object modeling tasks.

We have developed a numerical method using the complex Edwards-Anderson model to determine the critical behavior near the Yang-Lee edge singularity for all traditional positive $O(N)$ universality classes. Our findings from the $1000 \times 1000$ lattice simulations match the critical exponents previously established for the Yang-Thirumalai universality class at the Ising point, as well as for other universality classes with $0 < N \leq 2$. Our method allows us to estimate these exponents with high precision, specifically for $\beta = 0.375811(10)$, $\gamma = 1.08576(11)$, and $\gamma_{\rm log} = 0.45721(11)$.

In this work, we establish a lemma that extends the Sudakov-Fernique lemma to a stochastic process, thereby generalizing the nonconvexity of the TAP free energy's second derivative observed in recent studies. Utilizing this enhanced Sudakov-Fernique lemma, we provide an alternative proof of the local convexity of the TAP free energy's analytic continuation, as demonstrated by Benaych-Georges and Nardari. Furthermore, we apply this generalization to derive an expression for the second derivative of the TAP free energy that does not involve a probabilistic interpretation.

A new method is proposed to calculate the aerosol optical depth (τ) of a specific wavelength using the brightness of stars and their color indices. This approach leverages the relationship between the observed color of a star and the light it loses as it travels through the atmosphere. A key finding is that τ can be determined by the difference in color indices of a star observed through different parts of the atmosphere, one with a clear path and one through the layer containing the aerosols. This technique is demonstrated using astrophotography images of bright stars, and calculations are made for various wavelengths and atmospheric conditions. The results are compared to established relationships between τ and the color indices of stars, and it is shown that τ can be accurately calculated using this method. This approach is particularly useful for measuring τ in the upper atmosphere, where traditional methods are less effective.

To accurately estimate the complete six-degree-of-freedom pose of an object, it's essential to determine its orientation and position in 3D space. A key challenge lies in positioning, as it involves resolving the scale and translation of an object's point cloud based on its projected 2D image. To address this challenge, we developed a novel two-stage method called DeepHMap++ for pose estimation. In the first stage, our model employs a projection clustering network to generate a synthetic depth map that represents the object's position. In the second stage, we trained a correspondence learning network to refine the predicted position and scale by comparing the object's point cloud with the generated depth map. Our approach eliminates the need for expensive 3D convolutional layers and allows for the use of correspondence learning in the second stage. Our method achieved state-of-the-art results on three datasets, including a 10.1° mean absolute error on the NUS-View dataset, a 1.9cm mean absolute error on the SUN dataset, and a 10.5° mean absolute error on the TUM-FR2 dataset.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based tool designed to automate the computation of
the Generalized Graphical Lasso for a variety of conditional independence
testing scenarios, encompassing both binary and multi-class classifications and
regression. This package provides an efficient framework for working with
large-scale datasets and includes a range of established algorithms for
implementation, such as coordinate descent, block coordinate descent, and
ADMM. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GGLasso through a comprehensive
set of examples and comparative analyses with existing Python and R packages.

Molecular dynamics simulations are commonly used to investigate the behavior of molecules in various configurations. However, these simulations can be computationally intensive, making it challenging to explore a broad range of possible configurations. We have developed a novel approach to address this issue by employing simplified physics-based models that allow for a more efficient exploration of possible configurations. Our method uses a version of the Langevin dynamics algorithm that has been adapted to operate on a discrete grid system, enabling a faster and more accurate exploration of possible configurations. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it to other methods and showing that our method is both robust and reliable.

A novel approach to identifying influential nodes in multilayer networks is proposed, building on the concept of node prominence. A specific multilayer network framework is considered, where the connections between network layers are defined. A new metric, called node significance, is introduced to account for inter-layer connections. A prominence value is assigned to each node based on its centrality in individual networks and its significance. A method to detect prominent nodes is proposed using the Eigenvector Prominence algorithm. A theoretical analysis and a case study are conducted to validate the proposed approach.

This article provides a comprehensive proof of Dirac's theorem, originally established in 1963, which states that any three-dimensional Minkowski spacetime can be transformed into standard Minkowski spacetime through a coordinate transformation. To achieve this, we first derive the most general coordinate transformation for two-dimensional spacetimes, and subsequently apply this knowledge to prove the statement for three-dimensional spacetimes.

This study investigates the liquid entry surface seal (LESS) phenomenon for a sphere entering a liquid pool, extending previous research that primarily focused on the seal behavior of flat plates and cylinders. A sphere's entry speed significantly impacts the LESS phenomenon, and this research defines a new speed parameter to characterize this phenomenon. Experimental data shows that a sphere's LESS phenomenon can be categorized into three speed regimes: low, intermediate, and high. In the low speed regime, a vapor pocket forms and collapses, leading to the seal. In the intermediate regime, the vapor pocket is smaller and the seal occurs more quickly. In the high speed regime, the vapor pocket is even smaller and the seal occurs even faster. This research also defines a critical speed for the transition between the intermediate and high speed regimes. The entry speed of the sphere can be broken down into two components: the hydrodynamic entry speed and the Froude entry speed. The hydrodynamic entry speed is the speed at which the sphere enters the liquid pool, and the Froude entry speed is the speed at which the sphere enters the liquid pool relative to gravity. This research shows that the sphere's LESS phenomenon is primarily driven by the hydrodynamic entry speed. The critical speed for the transition between the intermediate and high speed regimes is found to be 1.5 m/s. This research also defines a new dimensionless speed parameter to characterize the sphere's LESS phenomenon. This parameter is found to be consistent with previous research that defined speed parameters for flat plates

We investigate the generic features of low-energy effective field theories in Type IIB string theory, incorporating instanton effects and non-perturbative contributions. By incorporating a specific basis of independent operators, we establish a framework to analyze the structure of F-terms and D-terms, which are responsible for breaking supersymmetry. We demonstrate that a particular class of $\theta$-terms, which are not protected by any symmetry, can contribute to breaking supersymmetry in a non-universal manner. We also examine the implications of this class of operators on the moduli space and the resulting vacuum expectation values.

Our study uses X-ray absorption spectroscopy to examine the electronic structure of 3d transition metal ions in cubanite CuFe2S3, focusing on Fe's K-edge. By comparing experimental data with theoretical calculations, we found that the Fe ions in cubanite exhibit orbital asymmetry, with a higher degree of 3d3 t2g orbital occupation than 3d2 eg orbital occupation. This finding is consistent with cubanite's metallic properties and is a characteristic of strongly correlated electron systems.

The interaction between an exciton and a quantum dot's fluctuating charge environment can lead to a significant energy shift, known as a Stark effect, which is particularly pronounced for dark excitons. This research demonstrates that applying a moderate electric field of 1.5 V/cm can cause the dark exciton's mass to effectively double, leading to a decrease in its oscillation frequency by a factor of two. By utilizing ultrafast laser pulses, we observed the dark exciton's mass dynamics without the need for a magnetic field, and found that a specific quantum state transition could be used to detect this behavior. Our findings provide a method for controlling dark exciton coherence through the application of an electric field, which could have significant implications for quantum information processing.

We investigate the electronic band structure of a two-dimensional electron lattice with a glide symmetry, exploring its unique non-symmorphic characteristics. By leveraging first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that this lattice exhibits Dirac cones at high symmetry points, which can be manipulated through spin-orbit coupling and lattice deformation. Our findings provide a framework for predicting and designing two-dimensional electronic lattices with glide symmetry that exhibit non-trivial topological properties.

Quantum light sources exhibiting non-classical characteristics, such as squeezed and Fock states, are essential for advancing quantum technologies. However, generating single-photon facilitated coherent states (SPFC) from a specific photon number to its adjacent coherent state with high efficiency and on-demand production remains a significant challenge. We propose a novel approach using quantum-optical catalysis to address this challenge. By employing a carefully designed beam splitter and a single-photon source, we demonstrate that SPFC states can be produced with high fidelity and yield. Our findings indicate that with optimal settings, the system can achieve up to 90% average photon number, 99% state purity, and 95% production yield. Notably, our approach is robust against imperfections in the beam splitter and single-photon source, making it a promising method for generating high-quality SPFC states.

This work re-examines the use of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism of General Relativity, initially outlining their role in describing gauge fields, particularly in the context of the Maxwell equations and the NP field equations. It then delves into the application of bivectors to the Riemann tensor, which serves as a foundation for the subsequent development of the Newman-Penrose formalism. A key aspect of this formalism is the construction of a complex self-dual representation of the Weyl tensor from two null tetrads, ultimately leading to the derivation of the 37 NP equations from the real Weyl tensor equations.

This research paper introduces a novel approach to extracting formal specifications from programs, specifically from a linear regression-based method for predicting polymers. The existing approach to predicting polymers involves using empirical data to fit a straight line, but our method utilizes a comprehensive dataset that includes both linear and curved line data. A curved line is represented as a polynomial of degree two, and our approach employs first-order logic and a type of whole programming called SMT-based code, to deduce the proposed regression method. The resulting formal specification can be applied to verify the correctness of alternative algorithms for predicting polymers.

Segmenting neoplasms in the esophagus from computed tomography images is a challenging task due to the irregular shape and low contrast of the tumors. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that combines a modified U-Net architecture with a custom-designed attention mechanism. Our approach, called DDAUnet, incorporates a dense block into the U-Net encoder to capture a broader range of features, and a novel attention mechanism to prioritize significant features. Experimental results on two public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming ten state-of-the-art methods in terms of Dice Similarity Coefficient and Hausdorff Distance.

The rise of the internet and social media has led to a significant increase in digital communication, which has given birth to new forms of language that often mix multiple languages. This code-switching and code-mixing phenomenon is prevalent among multilingual communities and is characterized by the integration of foreign words, grammatical structures, and even non-linguistic elements such as emojis and hyperlinks. Despite its prevalence, the challenges posed by code-mixing to Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks have not been thoroughly examined, particularly in the context of multilingual communities. This paper aims to fill that gap by exploring the factors that contribute to code-mixing and its implications for NLP tasks. Through the analysis of existing literature, case studies, and discussions with experts, we have identified key issues and proposed potential solutions to address the challenges posed by code-mixing. To facilitate future research, we have also developed an open-source library that includes code-mixed datasets and tools for NLP tasks.

Utilizing human reference information has been shown to significantly enhance various image-based tasks, yet its potential in improving image caption generation models remains unexplored. In this study, we investigate whether incorporating human reference data can enhance image caption generation models. Our findings reveal that models trained without utilizing human reference data achieve superior performance compared to those trained with it. Furthermore, we discover that pre-trained models' ability to interpret images is limited to recognizing prominent features, missing more subtle and significant details.

Tantalum oxide with the cristobalite structure is a unique form of Ta$_2$O$_5$ that exhibits interesting dielectric and optical properties. To fully understand and utilize this material, it is important to investigate its base state crystal structure. However, the current knowledge of Ta$_2$O$_5$ base state configurations is limited due to the scarcity of experimental data on its structure. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted first-principles calculations to determine the Ta$_2$O$_5$ base state configurations and found that the Ta$_2$O$_5$ base state configuration corresponds to the $\alpha$-cristobalite structure. To further explore the Ta$_2$O$_5$ base state configuration, we also performed Monte Carlo simulations to examine the stability of the $\alpha$-cristobalite structure. The results of these simulations showed that the $\alpha$-cristobalite structure is not the most stable configuration at 0K, but rather the $\beta$-cristobalite structure is the most stable configuration. This discrepancy between the $\alpha$-cristobalite and $\beta$-cristobalite structures may be explained by the presence of strong electron-phonon coupling in Ta$_2$O$_5$. The current study provides a comprehensive understanding of the Ta$_2$O$_5$ base state configurations and paves the way for further investigation of

Our study examines how geographic information influences the spread of fake news on Reddit in the United States. We developed a method to create false news stories with altered geographic details and conducted an experiment with 1,000 Reddit users to observe their reactions. Our findings indicate that when geographic information is removed or changed, users are more likely to share fake news stories. This effect is particularly pronounced among users from rural and southern regions of the US. Our results have implications for understanding the role of location in the spread of misinformation online and for designing interventions to reduce the impact of false news.

This research focuses on developing a detailed acoustic analysis of verbal guidance given by human instructors during the demonstration of manipulation tasks for robots. Unlike existing studies that primarily analyze instructional language in problem-solving contexts, our work specifically examines tasks involving physical manipulation of objects. Through the examination of 10 hours of instructional audio, we identified 14 distinct acoustic patterns, categorized into four groups: basic speech elements, feedback, attention-grabbing utterances, and descriptions of ongoing actions. These findings provide a foundation for future work in automatic guidance generation, including the creation of models to predict instructional patterns based on visual input and the development of systems capable of learning and replicating these patterns.

This research develops a geometric field theory that mirrors the complexity of gauge theory from first principles, rooted in differential geometry. Our approach involves differential algebra and the study of differential equations, particularly Euler-Arnold equations, which describe the motion of rigid bodies. We establish that gauge theory arises from differential algebraic Lie algebras, demonstrating that its inherent intricacy is a natural outcome. Our findings are applicable to both rigid body dynamics and fluid dynamics, the latter governed by hydrodynamics.

Conversational systems are increasingly used in customer service, but assessing their effectiveness is a complex task. This paper introduces an automated evaluation framework that streamlines the assessment process by automatically testing conversational bots using recorded user interactions. The framework can be easily adapted to evaluate different bots and datasets, and its modularity allows for easy customization. We demonstrate its utility by assessing two existing conversational bots, and the source code is made available on GitHub.

To enhance personalized recommendations, especially for users with limited interaction history, this study introduces a novel multi-domain cooperative recommendation framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR). The key component of MSDCR is an innovative thorough aspect preference learning mechanism that delves into multiple dimensions of user interests. This mechanism enables the exchange of knowledge between different domains, allowing for the sharing of sparse information across various aspects of user interests. The MSDCR model then leverages a cooperative learning strategy to integrate the knowledge gained from different domains, resulting in a more comprehensive understanding of user preferences. Theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate the MSDCR model's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art single and multi-domain recommendation techniques.

This work presents a new approach to conic optimization, introducing a family of solvers based on the Hypatia framework. These solvers, specifically the Newton-CG-Hypatia, MinRes-Hypatia, and Hypatia variants, are designed to handle large-scale problems efficiently by leveraging a preconditioned iterative method for solving the KKT system. Numerical experiments conducted on organic conic formulations demonstrate the effectiveness of these solvers, showing that they can achieve a 100x speedup compared to traditional methods when working with semidefinite cones of high dimensions.

This paper presents a new approach to address the challenge of learning from imbalanced data in MRI quality assurance classification. We identify a key factor contributing to data imbalance, which is the limited variability in high-quality images compared to low-quality ones. This key factor is used to develop a novel data augmentation method, which applies a range of transformations to high-quality images to increase their diversity. This approach is then applied to a generalization problem in MRI quality assurance, which is characterized by its multi-dimensional imbalance. We evaluate our method using two existing datasets and find that it outperforms existing data balancing techniques. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using a new dataset, which is based on MRI images from the Internet.

This research investigates how privately owned electric vehicles impact the resilience of power distribution networks during extreme weather events. It is hypothesized that private EVs can both hinder and enhance network resilience, depending on their charging habits. To examine this, a novel mathematical model is developed that accounts for the decision-making of private EV owners, who aim to minimize discomfort while considering the risk of power outages. This model is then applied to a test network, revealing how private EVs can exacerbate the effects of severe weather, particularly when charging during peak times. However, it is also found that strategic management of private EV charging can mitigate the effects of severe weather on network resilience. A key finding is that private EV owners can be incentivized to charge during peak times, thereby reducing the risk of power outages. This research highlights the importance of considering private EV behavior in assessing network resilience and demonstrates the potential benefits of using multi-agent optimization methods to achieve this goal.

This paper explores the challenge of constructing a multi-agent system capable of a repetitive task, specifically conducting two meetings with an individual in a three-step environment. The agent is required to navigate to a designated spot, communicate with the individual to learn a target color, and then locate an object of that color to bring back. We propose a modular architecture that allows each task to be addressed by a separate recurrent network, linked by an incentive system that utilizes the connections between tasks to facilitate learning. Our approach enables each network to focus on its specific task while leveraging shared knowledge to improve overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this design in both simulated and real-world settings.

This research delves into the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the solid solution GdxCm1-xSn3 using a first-principles approach within the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method. Our calculations indicate that both GdSn3 and CmSn3 adopt the CaAl3-type cubic structure with the space group $R\bar{3}m$. The Gd and Cm atoms occupy the 3a Wyckoff positions, while Sn atoms occupy the 6d positions. Our computed lattice constants and bulk moduli for GdSn3 and CmSn3 align closely with previous experimental and theoretical data. Our results reveal that GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit metallic behavior with a magnetic moment of 7.0 $\mu_B$ for GdSn3, which is in close agreement with the theoretical spin-only value of 7 $\mu_B$. The CmSn3 compound displays a magnetic moment of 3.0 $\mu_B$, which is lower than the spin-only value of 4 $\mu_B$ due to the contribution of the Cm 5f and Sn 5p orbitals. Our calculations also reveal that GdxCm1-xSn3 exhibits metallic behavior for both x=0.25 and x=0.5 compositions, with a magnetic moment of 5.0 $\mu_B$ for x=0.25 and 3.
A table is presented that outlines predicted quantities of extra baryons and mesons within various theories.

A key result in combinatorial theory known as the foundation theorem for a Coxeter group of the first kind has been extended to a broader class of Coxeter groups called C2n-Coxeter groups. This extension is significant as it provides a basis for the free Coxeter algebra of the B-type, which is a crucial component in the study of combinatorial structures. The proof of this generalized theorem relies on a specific property of Coxeter graphs, which allows for the decomposition of complex structures into simpler, more manageable components. This decomposition is achieved through a process called "cutting" the Coxeter graph, which is shown to preserve the combinatorial properties of the original structure. This result is shown to be equivalent to another combinatorial object called a braided line, which is a key component in the study of knot theory. This connection is established through a series of isomorphisms that link the combinatorial structures of Coxeter groups to the topological structures of braided lines. This result is shown to be a significant advancement in the study of combinatorial structures and their applications to topological theories.

A study has been conducted on the gravitational lensing effects of large-scale structures on Type Ia supernovae observed through the Pantheon dataset, consisting of 1057 supernovae from the past 6.5 billion years. By utilizing the observed brightness variations and comparing them to the expected distribution, an estimate of the cosmic deceleration parameter was derived, resulting in an initial value of q_0 = 0.44 ± 0.15. This value was subsequently adjusted to account for the impact of supernovae residing within dark energy voids, leading to an adjusted estimate of q_0 = 0.55 ± 0.15. This result is consistent with findings from other studies on the cosmic acceleration phenomenon.

This research presents a compact and efficient 3x3 220nm Si3N2 waveguide hub designed using a supermode-based method. The proposed hub has a low loss of 0.04dB and a small footprint of 100x100 um2. The study also includes the fabrication and experimental verification of the photonic integrated circuit, demonstrating the applicability of the supermode-based design method for high-performance silicon-on-insulator components.

Convolutional neural networks excel in identifying objects within images by leveraging contextual information. However, the underlying mechanisms behind this context utilization remain unclear. To investigate this, we developed a context assessment framework that employs a context-aware object detector, specifically a context-guided mask proposal network, to identify context regions in objects and backgrounds. Subsequently, we analyzed the context features within these regions using a variety of classification models. Our findings reveal that spatial context is a significant factor in object detection, with context classification accuracy surpassing that of object detection. Notably, context is primarily concentrated in object boundaries, and its effectiveness diminishes with an increase in object class complexity. Our results also demonstrate the transferability of context features across different object detectors. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenyux1997/COD.

This paper investigates a Kirchhoff-type elliptic equation featuring a singular Trudinger-Moser growth function and a Dirac mass at the origin. By utilizing a combination of variational principles and critical point theory, we establish the existence of two distinct solutions to this equation.

We investigate the relationship between negative correlation and concentration
inequalities for binary random variables defined on a measure space. Specifically,
we examine the conditions under which negative correlation implies that the sum
of these variables follows a sub-Gamma distribution. We find that for any space
with a diameter of at most d, the measure must satisfy a Poincar\'e inequality
with a constant of at most d to ensure this property. We also explore the
implications of log-Sobolev and convex-concavity inequalities on negative
correlation and demonstrate how these properties can be used to derive
concentration inequalities for functions that are both negatively correlated and
convex or concave. We provide examples of measures that satisfy these
inequalities and show how they can be applied to derive new results for the
uniform measure on the Hamming cube and the Stiefel manifold.

We introduce a new class of operations in symplectic geometry called "symplectic modifications," which generalize the concept of blowing up and blowing down. These operations involve removing a specific type of symplectic submanifold from a manifold and replacing it with a different one, while maintaining the symplectic properties of the overall manifold. We establish the functorial nature of these modifications under certain conditions and demonstrate how they can be used to analyze the relationship between different symplectic manifolds. Additionally, we explore the connection between symplectic modifications and other established operations, such as Gompf's connected sum along a sphere.

A method called "ideal acceptance" has been developed to assess how compatible incompatible kidneys are for transplantation. This approach uses a statistical model to determine the probability that a donor kidney will be accepted by a specific patient. The model was trained on data from 1,000 successful kidney transplants and tested on 1,000 additional cases. It was found that the model can accurately predict kidney compatibility, with the most compatible kidneys having a high acceptance rate of 99% and the least compatible having a rate of 1%. A key aspect of the model is its use of a time-dependent feature that accounts for the waiting time for a suitable kidney transplant. This information can be valuable for prioritizing kidney transplants and improving the success rate of incompatible kidney transplants.

We investigate whether the word embeddings used in NLP effectively capture the semantic meaning of words associated with high Loughran-McDonald scores, which represent positive sentiment, and low scores, which represent negative sentiment. Using a straightforward approach, we examine the relationships between word representations and their sentiment scores, and find that the magnitude of these relationships is quite low. Furthermore, we discover that the linear projections commonly used to interpret these representations fail to accurately reflect the non-linear nature of the sentiment scores. Our research also reveals that the distribution of sentiment scores is skewed and that the representations of positive and negative words are not clearly separated in the vector space. To address this issue, we propose a new metric that takes into account the non-linear properties of the scores and demonstrate that the word representations do not effectively distinguish between positive and negative words. Our findings have significant implications for the use of NLP in financial applications, where the accurate interpretation of sentiment is crucial.

This work extends the BWP framework by incorporating multiple data streams and OFDM technology, resulting in an expanded model that accounts for frequency-selective fading and time-varying channel conditions. Building on this generalized BWP model, we introduce optimization algorithms for jointly designing the RF waveform and digital signals in both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM scenarios. Numerical simulations are conducted to compare the BWP framework with conventional integrated data and power transmission methods.

This research presents an approach to modeling solidification and melting processes within a moving boundary, using the Navier-Stokes equations and the energy balance equation. The numerical method combines a mixed level-set and embedded boundary technique to track the boundary's movement, with temperature discretized using finite elements and velocity and pressure discretized on a Cartesian grid via an embedded boundary technique. The numerical scheme's stability is ensured through a conservative level-set reconstruction and a modified pressure projection method. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations of various test cases, including Stefan problems with one and multiple boundaries, and Rayleigh-Benard convection.

A key concept in game theory known as rationalizability, which is based on the assumption that players are strategic and believe others are too, can lead to a wide range of possible outcomes, as it does not necessarily result in a single equilibrium. This research aims to understand the conditions under which rationalizable behavior in a game leads to a specific set of outcomes that correspond to the rationalizable outcomes of its Bayesian game representations. The paper provides a characterization of this condition, called rationalizable equilibrium, and investigates its properties in relation to other solution concepts. Additionally, it explores the stability of this concept under small changes in the game and its relationship to other equilibrium concepts, such as the correlated rationalizability and the set of rationalizable actions. To further analyze this concept, the paper also examines its application to games with incomplete information and shows that it is equivalent to the correlated Bayesian rationalizable equilibrium in such cases. The paper also presents a method for implementing this concept in a multiplayer competition setting, where players are rewarded for actions that are consistent with the rationalizable equilibrium.

We investigate the dynamics of an SIS epidemic spreading through a network that undergoes structural changes to limit transmission. Initially, the network is a random configuration with no specific pattern, and infected individuals are given the option to alter their connections by severing links with infected peers and forming new ones with uninfected nodes. This self-directed strategy, known as protective rewiring, is driven by the desire to avoid further infection. Our study reveals that this adaptive behavior can significantly slow down the epidemic's progression, even when the transmission rate is high. In fact, for certain conditions, the protective rewiring can lead to a complete eradication of the epidemic, surpassing the threshold for disease persistence found in static networks. This phenomenon is also observed in networks where links have varying strengths, and we find that protective rewiring is most effective when the available stronger connections are limited.

We developed a unified approach to describe the evolution of parton distribution functions (PDFs) at a high-energy scale, incorporating experimental data at lower-energy scales. This approach treats PDFs as functions of a high-energy scale, subject to both perturbative and non-perturbative evolution equations. At a starting high-energy scale, the PDFs are determined from measurements at a lower-energy scale, utilizing both fixed-order and next-to-leading logarithmic approaches. We further explored the relationship between the starting high-energy scale and the lower-energy scale, and its impact on the determination of fundamental PDF parameters. This framework enables a systematic and consistent method for determining PDF parameters from various types of experimental data, including both fixed-order and resummation data. We applied this framework to analyze a range of data sets, including photon and low-x hadron data, and found that the starting high-energy scale for quarks and gluons is significantly higher than that for heavy quarks.

Reinforcement learning agents in complex environments often struggle due to limited data, which hinders their ability to learn effectively. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed experience replay, a technique that allows agents to reuse past experiences. However, existing methods for managing replay buffers fail to account for the variance in data samples, potentially leading to suboptimal policy improvements. This paper introduces a novel variance decrease based experience replay method, which optimizes the replay buffer's sampling strategy to minimize data variance. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate that this method can significantly enhance policy learning in both value-based and policy-based learning settings.

To better support diverse conversational contexts, we've developed MultiTalk, a model capable of predicting multiple valid next responses in a dialogue. Unlike existing models that only forecast the most probable single response, our approach uses a highly branching prediction system to generate a set of potential responses. We've enhanced this framework with a selective sampling method to optimize the quality of predicted responses. We've also introduced a new task called dialogue continuation, which involves predicting response sets given a conversation history. We've conducted extensive experiments on two datasets, showing that our model outperforms baseline methods in both single response and set prediction tasks.

We have developed a numerical code for N-body simulations of gravity theories that differ from standard general relativity, specifically a model where the Einstein-Cartan action is modified by an $R^2$ term and includes coupling to matter fields. This code allows for the quick generation of simulations for a wide range of parameters and cosmological conditions. It can generate $R^2$ parameter values, matter field initial conditions, and the Hubble parameter for simulations of various sizes and resolutions in a short amount of time. This efficiency is made possible by using an optimized strategy for generating and storing data, as well as parallel processing techniques. We have also created a new method for generating random number sequences that can be used to generate multiple simulations with different random number sequences in a single run. This code is a valuable tool for researchers studying the effects of altered gravity on the large-scale structure of the universe.

Building on Schramm's theory of multiple independent Brownian paths, we establish a connection between the Gaussian free field conditioned to vanish at its boundary and a specific subset of its natural driving fields. This subset corresponds to a class of measures that are absolutely continuous with respect to the Gaussian free field, and are characterized by their expected energy being finite. This relationship is further explored in the context of a specific class of measures known as log-Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, which are independent of one another and drive the paths in question.

MediaWiki, the underlying technology for Wikipedia, is a powerful tool for collaborative knowledge sharing.
However, its effectiveness in specialized fields, where in-depth understanding is crucial, is limited.
To address this issue, we developed WorkingWiki, a customized MediaWiki platform designed for our group's research collaboration.
WorkingWiki combines the collaborative features of MediaWiki with additional functionalities, such as LaTeX support,
real-time code execution, and interactive data visualization, to facilitate effective teamwork.
We will present the design and implementation of WorkingWiki, along with its source code,
and demonstrate its effectiveness through its application in our research project.

This study develops a computational model to simulate the interaction between a turbulent jet fire and an acoustic field within a linearized framework. The fire's thermoacoustic behavior is represented using a reduced-order flame description, and numerical simulations are conducted with a high-fidelity CFD code, FDS. The model's flame dynamics are based on a nonlinear polynomial, and its coefficients are determined through a genetic algorithm. The resulting reaction model is significantly more computationally efficient than traditional CFD approaches, enabling the simulation of large-scale fire and ducted combustion systems. The model's performance is validated against experimental data from a jet fire exposed to acoustic excitation in a linearized structure. The simulations accurately predict the flame's response, including the frequency and amplitude of vortex shedding, and the model's reaction coefficients are found to be consistent with previous studies.

The investigation of neutrino mass through the search for neutrinoless double beta decay in laboratory experiments, along with the analysis of neutrino behavior in astrophysical environments, has a common focus on neutrino mass and its impact on neutrinoless double beta decay. In this context, we examine the implications of an ultralight dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, which is a novel and promising area of research. We explore the effects of this interaction on the neutrinoless double beta decay process and the neutrino signal observed in direct dark matter detection experiments, particularly in the late stages of neutron star evolution. We also investigate the potential for this interaction to be detected through the observation of neutrinoless double beta decay in laboratory experiments. A key aspect of this research is the development of a framework that allows for a comprehensive analysis of the impact of this interaction on neutrinoless double beta decay, dark matter detection, and the evolution of neutron stars. This framework is implemented in the NeutrinoEncountersUltralightDSDM package, which enables researchers to explore the effects of this interaction in a systematic and efficient manner.

This research extends the nonlocal gravitational model by introducing a new class of underdetermined connections, referred to as constitutive connections, which are defined through a nonlocal relationship with the Riemann curvature tensor. A modified nonlocal gravitational theory is then developed using a new action functional, which incorporates an additional term that links the connection to a nonlocal essential tetrad field. When the action functional is varied with respect to the constitutive connections, a nonlocal constitutive equation is obtained, which allows for the connections to be expressed in terms of the essential tetrad field and a nonlocal curvature tensor. Substituting this expression into the nonlocal gravitational field equations yields a reformulated set of equations that are equivalent to the original nonlocal equations. A comparison is also made between this modified nonlocal gravitational model and a similar model based on a nonlocal Poincar\'e gauge theory of gravity.

This study integrates genomic functional annotations with results from genome-wide association studies for 18 human traits, including height, weight, blood pressure, cholesterol, and autoimmune diseases, using data from over 1.2 million individuals in the UK Biobank. By applying a Bayesian method, we identified 182 genomic regions with significant enrichment for trait-associated variants, with the highest enrichment found in regions containing genes that regulate chromatin structure and histone modification. The relationship between these regions and specific traits was further explored, revealing connections between certain genes and traits such as obesity and hypertension. The findings highlight the importance of integrating genomic functional information with genetic association studies to better understand the genetic basis of complex human traits.

This report provides an overview of various experimental analyses centered on
tiny systems produced in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, covering both
initial stages described by perturbative QCD and later stages involving non-
perturbative QCD. It covers investigations into photon and hadron production in
peripheral and central collisions, as well as the creation of quark-gluon plasma
in ultra-peripheral collisions.

The recurring outbursts of neutron star X-ray binaries are recurring.  They are caused by the accretion of matter from a companion star onto a neutron star.  The intervals between these outbursts vary greatly, from days to decades, and are influenced by the nature of the companion star.  The intervals between the outbursts of the dormant X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are not well understood.  We studied the recurring nature of 14 of these binaries, finding that 11 of them have intervals between outbursts that are not random.  The intervals between the outbursts of these binaries are recurring with periods ranging from 10 to 100 years.  The recurring nature of these binaries is not typical for low mass companion binaries, and is more characteristic of binaries with massive companion stars.  The nature of the Galactic Centre binaries is not well understood, and is thought to be due to the high density of the Galactic Centre.  We propose that the intervals between the outbursts of these binaries are recurring with periods ranging from 10 to 100 years, and that the nature of the Galactic Centre binaries is more characteristic of binaries with massive companion stars.

In quantum mechanics, a fundamental aspect of a system is described by a Hamiltonian, which includes various interactions between its components. A particular type of interaction, known as the vibrational anharmonicity, is responsible for enabling non-linear behavior in a system. This study focuses on a specific type of vibrational anharmonicity, called the electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational coupling due to momentum, which is found to be a universal feature of a wide range of physical systems. This coupling is shown to be a direct result of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and is demonstrated to be a more fundamental and general principle than the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. This study derives an explicit formula for this coupling, which is shown to be a second-order effect of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and is found to be a universal feature of a wide range of physical systems, including molecules, crystals, and quantum dots. This coupling is shown to be responsible for a variety of physical phenomena, including the breakdown of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, the emergence of non-linear behavior in a system, and the emergence of new types of anharmonicity in a system. This study also explores the implications of this coupling for a wide range of physical systems, including molecules, crystals, and quantum dots, and is found to be a key factor in the emergence of a variety of physical phenomena, including the emergence of non-linear behavior in a system, the emergence of new types of anharmonicity in a system

The concept of semantic entropy, which measures the diversity of vocabulary and phrasing used in a discourse, is explored in this study. We investigate the relationship between semantic variety in a conversation and Natural Language Inference (NLI) performance, specifically examining how NLI models can capture semantic information from a conversation. Our findings reveal that NLI models can effectively utilize the semantic information from a conversation, and that the addition of a hypothesis in the discourse increases the difficulty of inferring its meaning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pre-trained NLI models can capture the semantic information from a conversation, and that the use of a semantic control condition allows us to isolate the effect of semantic variety from other factors. Our study contributes to the understanding of how semantic information is captured and utilized in NLP tasks, and has implications for the design of more effective NLP models.

A numerical model was developed to simulate rotating sub-stellar bodies, taking into account the effects of rotation on their thermal evolution. The simulation includes a rotating frame of reference, centrifugal and Coriolis forces, and a mass-shedding limit, beyond which material would be lost from the equator. The model was used to investigate the impact of rotation on the internal structure, thermal evolution, and observable properties of brown dwarfs and giant planets. The results indicate that rapid rotation can lead to a significant decrease in effective temperature and luminosity, as well as an expansion of the radius, particularly in the early stages of evolution. The simulation also showed that the mass-shedding limit is reached at a critical rotation rate, which depends on the object's mass and age. The model was applied to a range of objects, including a 65 Jupiter-mass brown dwarf, a 10 Jupiter-mass planet, and a young planet in the system HD 10180. The results of the simulation can be used to interpret observations of rotating sub-stellar bodies and to guide future observations with next-generation telescopes.

This work presents an improved approach to incorporating measurement data that includes significant impact information in amplitude and phase parameter estimation for sinusoidal signals. A modification to the conventional impact information covariance matrix is proposed, which is then utilized in the least squares amplitude estimation algorithm. Numerical simulations demonstrate the benefits of this approach, showing that incorporating the impact information results in more accurate amplitude estimates compared to using the standard covariance matrix.

This research develops a comprehensive model for afterglows in gamma-ray bursts, incorporating a detailed analysis of the energy distribution and evolution of particle populations in the shock wave. By utilizing a computational approach, the study derives an explicit representation of particle populations over time and derives an expression for the afterglow spectrum that can be compared with observational data. The model reveals that the frequency associated with the electron acceleration threshold plays a critical role in determining the shape of the afterglow spectrum, and that this feature can be used to distinguish between different burst models. The study also identifies a new regime in which the afterglow spectrum is shaped by the interaction between the shock wave and the surrounding medium, and that this regime is characterized by a unique combination of frequency and time scales. The model provides a framework for interpreting observational data and for testing different burst models, and that it can be used to guide future observations and theoretical developments.

Given a graph G and an integer k, our goal is to divide the vertices of G into two separate parts, A and B, such that B forms a subgraph with at most k edges, and the size of A is as large as possible. This problem is related to parameterized graph theory, where we aim to maximize the size of A in relation to a given parameter. We demonstrate that the size of A can be at least the second power of the number of paths in the subgraph formed by B, plus an additional unit, which is a significant improvement over the previously established limit of the size of A being directly proportional to the number of edges in the subgraph formed by B. This new bound is a notable advancement in our understanding of the relationship between the size of A and the parameter p.

This paper introduces a propulsion-assisted locomotion framework designed to enhance the efficiency and resilience of bipedal robots. By incorporating a linear actuator in the shank of each leg, the system can generate forward propulsion, thereby reducing the need for recovery steps when encountering obstacles. To achieve this, we developed a hybrid zero-moment point controller that optimizes the timing and magnitude of propulsion assistance. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we conducted simulations using a three-degree-of-freedom leg model and a linear actuator, demonstrating significant improvements in both the efficiency and obstacle-negotiation capabilities of the robot.

Let $K$ be a field that extends the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, and also includes an algebraically closed version of its field of constants. We define a "respected field" as one where there exist specific elements that, when raised to a power of $p$, equal given elements in the field, except for those in the squared part of the field. We also define a "complete residue map" as one where every element in the field can be expressed as the $p$-th power of another element plus a part in the squared part of the field. We prove that if the characteristic of $K$ is not 2 or 3, and $K$ has a complete residue map, then it must include an algebraically closed version of its field of constants. We also provide examples of respected fields and show that the field of complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ does not have a complete residue map.

HyperDegrade is a novel dynamic DVFS strategy designed to optimize system
performance during gradual workload deterioration.  As applications experience
increasing levels of degradation, their effective processing speeds decline,
posing a significant challenge to maintain optimal performance.  Traditional
DVFS methods, which rely on adjusting CPU frequencies, are shown to be
ineffective in managing this issue.  Our research demonstrates that
performance management can be effectively achieved by manipulating scheduling
parameters, specifically by adjusting the time window for performance
evaluation.  HyperDegrade leverages this insight to automatically detect and
address performance declines, adjusting the evaluation time window to
minimize performance loss.  Our experimental results show that HyperDegrade
outperforms the state-of-the-art DVFS methods, achieving up to 1.5x better
performance with only a 1.5% overhead in energy consumption.  Our findings
also reveal that HyperDegrade is highly efficient, capable of being implemented
on current CPUs with a 1.5% overhead in energy consumption.

We have developed a novel method to unknot traditional and welded links, which involves transforming them into 4-valent graphs embedded in either $\mathbb{R}^2$ or $\mathbb{R}^3$. By applying our proposed sequence of moves, we can systematically eliminate all knots and crossings from these graphs. This achievement can be mathematically proven using the properties of the Jones polynomial, which serves as a powerful topological invariant for distinguishing between different types of knots and links.
We demonstrate that the Fox-Hatcher loop constitutes a Vassiliev characteristic of order three, and we fully describe its associated invariant space, which is three-dimensional.

This study focuses on developing a tactical collaborative framework for traditional robots with limited computational and communication capabilities. We propose a collaborative tactic structure that is divided into three distinct phases: data gathering, hypothesis generation, and action execution. During the data gathering phase, robots collect information from their surroundings and share it with their peers. In the hypothesis generation phase, they analyze the collected data to form potential solutions, prioritizing the most promising ones. In the action execution phase, they take actions based on their hypotheses, with a clear plan of action and a way to adjust if things don't go as expected. We tested our framework in a simulated scenario where robots had to locate and capture a target in a complex environment. The results showed that our collaborative tactic structure significantly improved the robots' performance compared to individual efforts.

This paper explores the concept of pragmatic privacy breaches in the context of
vertical federated learning (VFL), where multiple institutions collaborate to
train a machine learning model while keeping their local data private. We
examine several privacy threats that can be mounted against VFL systems,
including membership inference, reconstruction, and model inversion attacks.
These attacks are analyzed in relation to the VFL architecture and existing
privacy-preserving protocols, revealing that current methods do not always
guarantee data protection. Furthermore, we propose countermeasures to mitigate
these threats and provide Python-based demonstrations of membership inference
and reconstruction attacks on the FATE VFL platform.

In this paper, we introduce a novel kernel estimation method that utilizes
pseudo random Fourier attributes to automatically determine the optimal kernel
and bandwidth. This technique is particularly useful in non-parametric density
estimation, where it outperforms traditional kernel density estimation. Our
estimator is consistent and exhibits the same convergence rate as conventional
kernel density estimation. To validate our approach, we conducted simulations
and compared our results with standard kernel density estimation. Furthermore,
we applied our method to real-world data from the 1995 General Social Survey,
demonstrating its effectiveness in estimating population distributions.

This research focuses on embedding a specific group, denoted as Gamma, into a product space consisting of various hyperbolic garland components through a Cartesian decomposition. By breaking down a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold M with a non-trivial first homology into a product of hyperbolic garland components, we can analyze and embed Gamma within a corresponding product space. The components of M are decomposed using Thurston's hyperbolic structure theorem, and Gamma's embedding into each component is established using results from previous studies. The overall strategy involves systematically embedding Gamma into each hyperbolic garland component of the product space.

We prove a new property of a conformal hypersurface $\Sigma$ within the sphere $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$, demonstrating that its Mobius curvature is bounded below. Specifically, we establish that $\Delta H^2 \leq 4(Ric(\Sigma) - \frac{1}{n}(\delta H)^2)$, where $H$ represents the mean curvature, $\delta H$ is its gradient, and $Ric(\Sigma)$ is its Ricci curvature. Furthermore, if there exists a point where $Ric(\Sigma) = \frac{1}{n}(\delta H)^2$, we show that $\Sigma$ is conformally equivalent to a round hypersphere.

This research investigates the optimal allocation of time and power in a wireless communication system that uses simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT). In this system, a base station transmits information signals and harvests energy from a single antenna, while a second antenna collects only energy from the environment. The goal is to maximize the sum rate of the users while ensuring a minimum harvested energy threshold is met and a specific time is allocated for energy collection. By formulating this problem, we discover that the harvested energy threshold is not constant but rather a function of the data rate, which allows us to simplify the original problem into a more manageable form. This reformulated problem can then be efficiently solved using a combination of convex optimization and bisection search techniques. Furthermore, we explore the impact of various system parameters on the performance of the proposed algorithm.

We developed a new method to analyze the growth patterns of complex systems, specifically applying it to the growth of Cayley graphs. Our technique, known as avalanche scaling, measures changes in system growth in response to small perturbations, such as adding new edges or removing generators. By examining the relationship between the size increase and the magnitude of induced changes, we were able to determine the fractal dimension of complex systems. We used this method to investigate the growth patterns of Cayley graphs for the symmetric group Sn with different sets of generators, specifically all 3-cycles and transpositions. Our findings revealed that the size increase of these graphs follows a fractal pattern with dimensions of 4/3 and 3/2, respectively.

The detection sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is significantly limited by the movement of their mirrors in response to high-frequency gravitational waves. To address this issue, we propose a novel design called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which uses two masses connected by a spring to form an anti-parallel oscillator system. This design allows the masses to move in opposite directions, effectively increasing the displacement caused by gravitational waves and enhancing the detection sensitivity. We demonstrate that this new design can be integrated into existing detection systems without any major modifications, and we also propose a modified readout scheme called the dual-shearing Mach-Zehnder interferometer to fully utilize the increased detection range. This new design and readout scheme can be used to improve the high-frequency detection capabilities of current gravitational wave detectors without any major modifications.

In multi-user wireless networks, users' transmission areas can overlap, leading to interference and reduced data rates. This paper proposes a novel approach to eliminate overlapping transmission areas by utilizing a stochastic access protocol and advanced beamforming techniques in wireless systems with a vast number of antennas. The approach is modeled as a stochastic geometry problem, and its performance is analyzed using mathematical formulas. The results show that the proposed method can effectively prevent transmission area overlap, leading to improved data rates and reduced interference. The approach is also flexible and can be adapted to different system configurations.
